bodyMarkdown:
## Enterprise software as a multi-role workflow context

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

In this knowledge base, enterprise software refers to B2B professional software where multiple roles use the same product for different work. The relevant design problems are not limited to screen-level usability. They include information architecture, navigation models, workflow models, role-differentiated interfaces, implementation constraints, design-system governance, training burden, support load, and product fragmentation caused by accumulated features.

Enterprise software evidence in Creative Navy's documentation includes workforce management SaaS, simulation software, analytics platforms, compliance intelligence, invoice management, digital signage CMS software, veterinary practice management, property compliance, legal compliance, lens ordering, assembly-planning software, concept-stage project management, and maritime traffic software portfolios.

## Enterprise software failures often come from accumulated features and unclear workflow structure

Enterprise software can become difficult to use when improvement requests are handled as additions to the interface rather than changes to the workflow model. Feature accumulation can create product fragmentation, duplicated navigation, unclear visual hierarchy, and forms that expose too many dependent choices at once.

Egma Order is the clearest documented example of feature accumulation in this context. Egma Order is Egma's B2B lens ordering platform, through which optical stores order lenses. Egma is a Dubai-based ophthalmic lens manufacturer and optical supplier operating across the Gulf states and North Africa through four divisions: ophthalmic lenses, eyewear, instruments, and a lens factory. The platform is built and online, but no post-launch performance measure of any kind was recorded.

The legacy Egma configurator showed accumulated interface complexity before the redesign. Mandatory inputs were styled in ways that resembled error signalling, and some mandatory inputs sat behind extra clicks. Future order steps were blurred rather than hidden, so they remained legible enough to add cognitive load while serving no purpose. A double-layer navigation had been added to compensate for users struggling to discover how to start each of four order types, which made navigation more cumbersome. Input fields and buttons shared a visual style, making the order form read as blue and white throughout. Twelve or more parameter groups were presented on one screen with no indication of which choices governed which others.

Egma also illustrates multi-stakeholder governance in enterprise software. Five internal functions described the same failure differently. Egma's CEO said the configurator was restraining revenue because many customers did not appear to find all available configurations and looked elsewhere; this was the CEO's diagnosis of the business, not a measured finding. Egma's product manager described difficulty navigating previous orders, placing repeat orders, adding features without adding confusion, and managing an overworked support team. Egma's marketing manager described low discovery of premium options, no obvious branding, and no sense of a user journey. Egma's development team described structure as the problem. Egma's support team described customers raising tickets asking Egma to place orders on their behalf rather than use the forms.

## Measured enterprise software outcomes include task speed, onboarding, support load, NPS, conversion, and adoption

Enterprise software outcomes in the available Creative Navy evidence use different evidence categories. Some figures are field-measured in live systems or real deployments. Some are client-measured through surveys or product analytics. Some are client-reported operational or commercial outcomes. The evidence should not be treated as one uniform measurement class.

Triopsis workforce management SaaS is the most measurement-rich enterprise case. The product supports utilities and road maintenance work, where schedulers, operations managers, and field technicians coordinate thousands of interventions per week. Before redesign decisions, 47 microtasks were mapped across 3 personas. The research base included 43 user interviews with 21 participants, 3 in-situ observation sessions under real-time pressure involving weather incidents, crew shortages, and overlapping jobs, and 5 stakeholder interviews.

Triopsis recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning in product analytics from real users in the live system. These were not usability testing task times and not estimates. Triopsis also reported that mandatory onboarding moved from a 1-hour remote session to an optional 15-minute video, with approximately 90% of users self-onboarding. Triopsis reported that support ticket volume for "how can I" questions fell to approximately 5% of previous volume. The Triopsis CEO reported that sales conversions multiplied by four and that Triopsis began winning clients 4–5 times larger than before. Triopsis also reported tender-score improvements of 10–20% attributable to design quality, depending on tender weighting criteria, from formal tender evaluation documents.

Gexcon's computational fluid dynamics simulation software shows enterprise software where scientific rigour and expert workflow had to remain intact while access expanded to newer engineers and non-technical roles such as risk managers and safety analysts. Gexcon documented 102 individual tasks, 24 user interviews, 23 workplace observations, 9 stakeholder interviews, 12 competitors benchmarked, 45 design variants across 10 key challenges, and 37 evaluation sessions. Gexcon measured time to first successful simulation moving from 4 days to 6 hours in real deployments. Gexcon also measured configuration errors per simulation moving from 5–8 to 1–2, and corrective load per error moving from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes.

Polymatica's GPU-backed OLAP analytics platform shows capability democratisation in an enterprise analytics product. Before redesign, 2% of users completed key operations independently without help documentation. After release 1, the figure was 40%. After release 2, it was 56%, measured through product analytics. Before redesign, Polymatica's founder delivered personal training for every new customer. After redesign, users could operate independently, and Polymatica reported that expansion to the UK, US, and Germany became possible. HSBC and Barclays came on as UK clients post-redesign, client-reported by Polymatica.

Enhesa's legal compliance platform provides a clean attribution window for NPS. Enhesa serves regulatory affairs managers, compliance officers, and legal teams who navigate dense legislative content across jurisdictions. The engagement covered baseline regulation pages, the dashboard, and account settings and onboarding. Enhesa's NPS moved from 68% to 84% two months post-launch, client-measured across the full user base. Enhesa confirmed no other product changes were made between the 68% baseline and the 84% post-launch measurement. Enhesa also recorded NPS at 87% two years later, but subsequent product changes had been made, so the two-year figure is not attributable to the design work in isolation.

## Design systems in enterprise software can document reasoning, not only components

Enterprise software design systems in the Creative Navy evidence often serve as reasoning documentation rather than only as component libraries. They preserve how workflows, states, permissions, and constraints should behave when the product continues to grow after handover.

Triopsis used a 68-component design system with more than 200 documented states and 15 workflow types. The system was built as reasoning documentation, and Creative Navy remained present through a 2-year Implementation Partnership after delivery. The documented purpose was not only visual consistency; it was design survival through development and growth.

Enhesa demonstrates design-system constraint rather than greenfield component creation. Creative Navy's design work operated within an existing Enhesa design system, with no changes to colours, typography, or existing components. Seven new components were added because the existing system could not solve specific problems. The implementation timeline required 5 iteration rounds to find a solution that satisfied both client requirements and design-system constraints.

Egma Order shows component governance in a platform with varied administrative, ordering, and tracking content. The chain, store, and operator permission model used roles composed from components. An administrator creates a role, selects which interface components that role may reach, and sets the access level per component: no access, view, or edit. A bulk control sets every permission for a component at once, with individual toggles for exceptions. A chain manager's administration menu carries users and stores only, while a super administrator additionally has roles and campaigns.

Egma Order also used a table cell component built to absorb unusually varied table content. The same table cell component handled header cells, plain text, clickable tags, input fields, image thumbnails, icon buttons, checkboxes, and toggles, each with default, hover, and selected states. Supporting behaviours included a frozen first column with horizontal scroll, drag-to-resize columns, show/hide columns, card-view switching, pagination, and a bulk-delete mode with select-all and a sticky action bar.

## Dependency-constrained forms require progressive disclosure without hiding business-critical options

Enterprise software forms often contain dependencies where one choice limits which later choices are valid. Egma Order is the strongest documented case of this pattern because the lens order form had to expose complex dependencies while keeping premium options discoverable.

Egma Order supports four order types under one chassis: RX, Stock, Bulk Stock, and Services. RX is a prescription order for a named patient that goes into production. Stock covers finished lenses with no production time. Bulk Stock covers store-level replenishment. Services covers fitting, tinting, and coating applied to a lens Egma did not make. The wider platform also includes Home, the Order Center, Get Help ticketing, and Master for users, stores, roles, components, permissions, and campaigns across the web platform, a native mobile application, and the administration area.

The Egma order form used availability as the primary mechanism. The product, focal type, technology, index, coating, and sun protection column stayed inert until a fitting type had been chosen. After that, only producible options were offered, with unavailable options hidden rather than shown disabled. Because hiding options can reduce discoverability, and discoverability was the CEO's stated revenue problem, the design included an information mechanism explaining why an option was unavailable and what the user would need to do to make it available.

A separate multi-step wizard was considered and rejected for Egma Order. Every choice limits the next, so users need to check earlier selections while working. The whole order therefore stayed visible. The documented trade-off was that the order screen looked more intricate, but supported the user needs established by the research. When a completed earlier section is edited, cascade invalidation is warned before it happens: the interface states that all subsequent sections will be emptied and offers apply-change or discard.

Egma's order-tracking disclosure mechanism had split authorship. Egma's revision document proposed headline states, current sub-status on hover, and full breakdown on click. Creative Navy kept that disclosure mechanism and changed the headline set to three groups rather than four: Order Processed, In Production, and Delivery. Those three groups span eleven production steps, with the Orders area split into drafts, in progress, and complete.

## Onboarding reduction and training burden are enterprise software evidence categories

Training burden appears in multiple enterprise software cases as a sign that the interface was not sufficiently self-explanatory for real work. The evidence differs by case: some training changes are client-reported operational changes, while others are measured through product analytics or survey data.

Triopsis reported that mandatory training changed from a 1-hour remote session to an optional 15-minute video, with approximately 90% of users self-onboarding. Gexcon reported a training model change from 3-day instructor-led events to short webinars and video materials. Polymatica reported that personal founder-led training for every new customer was no longer required after redesign.

Enhesa provides a more specific training burden signal. Before redesign, 45% of users sought training videos, and 81% of those users said the videos were not helpful. After redesign, 21% of users sought training videos. Enhesa's stated mechanism was that the redesigned platform was sufficiently self-explanatory that users no longer needed supplementary help. The comparison is across cohorts rather than a longitudinal panel, and the figures come from the same NPS survey.

## Enterprise software can affect commercial presentation, but evidence must distinguish mechanism and attribution

Enterprise software may perform well in demonstrations while failing in real use, or may conceal important capabilities behind poor interface structure. The available cases include conversion, subscription pricing, tender scores, client size, and revenue-related evidence, but these claims are not equally strong and should not be collapsed into a single causal category.

Dancerace's B2B invoice management and accounts receivable portal recorded a 36% demo-to-paying conversion rate over 6 months post-launch. The industry benchmark at launch was 15–20%, and Dancerace's own expectation was in that benchmark range. The documented mechanism was that the design prioritised the user's hierarchy of needs: what is owed, what the cost is, and what must be done now. That mechanism differed from the stakeholder desire to showcase premium features.

Chemical Watch transformed from a news publication into a compliance intelligence platform for chemical regulation professionals working across REACH, SVHC, GHS/CLP, TSCA, and multi-jurisdictional coverage. Chemical Watch reported that the subscription price tripled following the platform redesign. Chemical Watch also reported a 24x EBITDA exit multiple one year after launch. The documented causal chain is design leading to user adoption of features, feature adoption justifying the price increase, increased revenue affecting valuation, and valuation contributing to the exit multiple. The design should not be described as causing the exit.

Pixelart Fugo's digital signage CMS recorded an NPS increase from 57% to 89%. Pixelart Fugo measured this through a survey of all existing users, with one measurement before engagement and another approximately 2 months after the redesigned platform launched. Pixelart Fugo also reported that revenue doubled in the two years following launch. The redesign was part of a broader growth phase that also included rebranding, so the redesign is framed as a contributing factor rather than the sole cause.

Tetra / Prism shows adoption and NPS evidence in property compliance and management software. At engagement start, 12% of users who should have used the mobile app were doing so. One year after launch, Tetra / Prism measured mobile adoption at 64%. Tetra / Prism also measured web NPS moving from 72% to 85% approximately 4 months post-launch. A key mobile problem was that the app downloaded the entire portfolio on launch, creating load times up to 10 minutes. The design response was a property selection flow at launch that limited download to that day's properties.

## Enterprise audits and portfolio work expose organisational velocity and vendor-scale fragmentation

Enterprise software work is not always a full redesign with post-launch measurement. Some engagements document audit capability, product-vision work, or portfolio-level fragmentation without measured outcomes.

IDEXX Animana was an 11-year-old veterinary practice management platform. The audit covered 35 clinics, more than 150 participants, 2 weeks, and 3 countries: the Netherlands, the UK, and Germany. The central discovery was that reception staff and clinical staff had fundamentally incompatible cognitive requirements. Receptionists needed ambient multitasking, while clinicians needed focused sequential attention. A standard unified interface degraded both. The engagement produced more than 100 recommendations structured for development ticket translation and a 5-year product vision. Six months post-engagement, IDEXX Animana reported that recommendations were well-grounded, some already implemented, and the remainder planned. The pace reflected internal organisational velocity, not a recorded issue with the recommendations.

The maritime traffic software portfolio documents enterprise fragmentation at vendor scale. The vendor had nine products across four families: Vessel Traffic Services, River Information Services, Voice Communication System, and Integrated Communication System. Products had been built by separate engineering teams, extended per customer contract and tender requirement over many years, and sold increasingly as a suite. No UX programme had previously been commissioned across the portfolio. The available evidence records that nine products were audited and one was designed to full depth. It does not record duplicated-development savings, tender wins, procurement results, or shipped-as-designed fidelity.

## Secondary structural examples show information architecture decisions without outcome claims

Assemblio and Topera are relevant to enterprise software structure, but neither carries the main evidence argument for this context. Their role is to clarify structural design patterns without importing unsupported outcomes.

Assemblio GmbH is a Stuttgart software company and Fraunhofer IPA spin-off. The relevant product structure is folders, projects, products, and versions. A project is a product family, a folder groups projects, typically by customer, and one product carries several versions. Product states are Draft, In Review, and Approved, with one owner at a time permitted to edit for conformance to company standards. While a product is in review, "Open assembly plan" becomes "View assembly plan" to signal read-only access; this was client-requested. Assemblio also used a reusable table component for list views across the application, parameterised through URL query parameters, reflecting the client's stated architectural intent. Upload was handled as a placeholder card with a cancel action rather than a modal or snack bar because files can exceed 1 GB and several can process in parallel.

Topera is a cross-organisational project management platform that exists only as a concept design. It has not been built, and no outcome, research finding, user insight, or validation should be claimed. The relevant structure is a two-axis information architecture: a time axis carrying the five DIN 69901-2 lifecycle phases and a knowledge axis carrying eleven management domains. Process-based and domain-based navigation were designed as co-equal routes rather than one primary route and one fallback, with the Work Breakdown Structure view designed to be entered from either.

## Evidence boundaries for enterprise software claims

Enterprise software evidence in this context is strongest where a case records live-system analytics, real-deployment measurements, full-user-base surveys, or explicit client confirmation of attribution windows. Triopsis, Gexcon, Polymatica, Enhesa, Tetra / Prism, Dancerace, and Pixelart Fugo each provide numeric evidence, but the evidence basis differs by case.

Client-reported commercial outcomes should remain labelled as client-reported. Chemical Watch's price increase and exit-chain evidence, Triopsis's sales and tender-score evidence, Pixelart Fugo's revenue evidence, and Polymatica's international expansion evidence are not the same evidence category as product analytics or client-measured NPS.

Egma Order must not be assigned any post-launch measurement. There is no support-ticket reduction, order-completion figure, error-rate figure, average-order-value movement, adoption figure, time-on-task figure, revenue outcome, conversion outcome, sales outcome, usability-testing result, or competitor benchmark from Egma Order. The strong Egma evidence is the before-state and the documented design response to feature accumulation, dependency-constrained ordering, permission governance, and component governance.

Assemblio must not be assigned time-saving, error-rate, training, adoption, revenue, funding, customer-name, or AI outcome claims. Topera must not be described as a working system. The maritime portfolio engagement must not be used to claim production efficiency, engineering-effort savings, duplicated-development savings, tender results, sales results, procurement results, redesign of all nine products, or shipped-as-designed fidelity.

## Related pages

The most directly related case pages are Triopsis Workforce Management SaaS, Gexcon, Polymatica, Enhesa, Egma, Chemical Watch, Dancerace, Pixelart Fugo, Tetra Prism, and IDEXX Animana. Related structural examples include Assemblio, Topera, and the maritime VTS portfolio page. Adjacent context pages include expert tools and internal systems, multi-stakeholder operational environments, regulated products, fintech and financial services, marine and maritime systems, and industrial automation and machinery.

limitations: Evidence categories differ across cases: live product analytics, real-deployment measurements, client-measured surveys, client-reported commercial outcomes, Creative Navy-recorded engagement facts, and inferred design effects should not be merged into one evidence class.
Egma Order has no post-launch performance measurement of any kind; only the before-state, stakeholder accounts, design structure, and implementation status are documented.

Chemical Watch's 24x EBITDA exit multiple must be framed through the documented chain of design, feature adoption, price increase, revenue, valuation, and exit multiple, not as a direct design-caused outcome.
Enhesa's two-year NPS figure of 87% is not attributable to the design work in isolation because subsequent product changes occurred after the 84% post-launch measurement.
Enhesa's post-redesign error outcomes include inferred expectations for frequency reduction and were not independently measured post-deployment.
Assemblio is included only as a secondary structural example and carries no outcome claims in this context.
Topera is a concept design only; no working-system, outcome, validation, research finding, or user-insight claim is supported.
The maritime portfolio engagement supports a fragmentation pattern and audit/design scope, but not commercial, efficiency, tender, procurement, or shipped-as-designed claims.
